research_notes.text: This is the public demo of the workbench: 12 made-up patients generated by a script, unrelated to any real case.

Once a node is selected, only admissions discharged before the node admission are shown; switching to the full course, opening the follow-up course or the treatment map is logged and saved with the Layer B record.

The real workbench chats with Claude or OpenAI. Here, preset scripts simulate streaming answers. The “node brief” for TACE node #3 of patient P-9615… and the AI analysis in its treatment map are pre-recorded real model output (also about made-up data), shown here in English translation.
Summary results of the ongoing study are unpublished and not shown in the demo.

public_evidence.text:
## Scope of the search and key conclusions

**Searched up to 24 November 2026.** Based only on guidelines and original studies, mainly the EASL 2025 guideline, the AASLD 2023 practice guidance and the 2026 Pan-Asian adapted ESMO guideline, supplemented by the 2024 Chinese guideline and related randomised trials; no specific patient is involved.

**Treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) does not follow a fixed order of “resection → ablation → intervention → systemic therapy”. Treatment is chosen by tumour extent, liver function and general condition together, and patients are re-triaged after response assessment.** At an early stage, cure comes first; at the intermediate stage, selective intervention is assessed; with vascular invasion, extrahepatic metastasis, or when intervention is unsuitable or no longer beneficial, the systemic-therapy path applies. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

## 1. Baseline assessment needed for every path

| Dimension | Information needed |
|---|---|
| **Diagnosis and tumour burden** | Multiphase contrast CT or MRI: lesion size, number and distribution, vascular invasion and extrahepatic metastasis; pathology is needed when non-invasive diagnostic criteria are not met. AFP alone cannot confirm the diagnosis. |
| **Liver reserve** | Bilirubin, albumin, coagulation, kidney function; Child–Pugh class together with ALBI/MELD; ascites, hepatic encephalopathy and previous decompensation. |
| **Portal hypertension** | Platelets, splenomegaly, varices and bleeding history; further portal pressure measures where needed. |
| **General condition** | ECOG performance status, comorbidities, nutrition and frailty, and treatment tolerance. |
| **Overall decision** | Record the BCLC stage and discuss in a multidisciplinary team of hepatology, surgery, interventional radiology, oncology and imaging; the stage does not replace assessment of technical feasibility and liver reserve. |

This assessment should be repeated at each treatment switch, not only at diagnosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

## 2. Four main treatment paths

### 1. Liver resection: both “can it be removed” and “can the remaining liver cope”

**Main conditions**
- HCC without cirrhosis that is confined and technically resectable.
- With cirrhosis, the typical conditions are limited tumour burden, well-compensated liver function, no clinically significant portal hypertension, and enough remaining liver. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10663390/?utm_source=openai))

**Key assessments**
- Relation of the tumour to major vessels and bile ducts, and whether complete resection is possible.
- Expected remnant liver volume and function, extent of resection, portal hypertension and perioperative risk.
- EASL allows minimally invasive minor resection in carefully selected patients with mild liver impairment or portal hypertension; **this does not mean major hepatectomy is also safe**. A large single tumour should not be excluded from resection on diameter alone. ([easlcampus.eu](https://easlcampus.eu/sites/default/files/2025-02/EASL_CPG_Management_HCC.pdf))

**After surgery**
- Assess recurrence risk from margins, microvascular invasion, satellite nodules and differentiation; AASLD recommends contrast CT/MRI every 3–6 months. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10663390/?utm_source=openai))

### 2. Ablation: an important curative option for early, small tumours

**Main conditions**
- Radiofrequency or microwave ablation suits early small HCC, especially **≤3 cm in patients who cannot or do not want to have surgery**.
- For compensated cirrhosis with a single tumour ≤2 cm and no transplant plan, EASL lists both resection and thermal ablation as recommended options; if resection would sacrifice a lot of liver parenchyma, ablation is preferred. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10663390/?utm_source=openai))

**Key assessments**
- Whether the whole tumour can be covered with an adequate safety margin.
- The needle path, and the distance to major vessels, central bile ducts, the gut and the diaphragm.
- Above 3 cm or in an unfavourable location, complete ablation and local control become harder; combined treatment, radiation segmentectomy or stereotactic radiotherapy can be discussed, and the decision should not rest on size alone. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

### 3. Intervention: TACE, TARE and HAIC are different

| Type | Conditions and role | Key assessments |
|---|---|---|
| **TACE: transarterial chemoembolization** | Mainly for intermediate-stage HCC confined to the liver that cannot be cured; best when liver function is adequate, portal flow is preserved and lesions can be treated selectively. | Tumour burden and infiltration, portal vein patency, feeding arteries, treatable liver volume and risk of decompensation. |
| **TARE: transarterial radioembolization, usually yttrium-90** | An alternative to TACE in some cases; radiation segmentectomy can also be used for confined lesions unsuitable for thermal ablation. | Angiography and shunt assessment, dose to normal liver, risk to non-target organs and liver reserve. |
| **HAIC: hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy** | Has a place in Chinese and other Asian guidelines, usually discussed for large intrahepatic burden, portal vein tumour thrombus or poor response to TACE; not a globally agreed first choice. | Intra- and extrahepatic disease distribution, liver function, catheter conditions and chemotherapy tolerance. |

The roles of TACE and TARE follow European, American and Pan-Asian guidelines; for HAIC, note the differences between regional guidelines and study populations. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

**When to stop repeating TACE?**  
If there is still no meaningful response after 1–2 adequate sessions, if vascular invasion or extrahepatic progression appears, or if liver function worsens, systemic therapy and other options should be discussed again, so that repeated intervention does not use up liver reserve. ([easlcampus.eu](https://easlcampus.eu/sites/default/files/2025-02/EASL_CPG_Management_HCC.pdf))

**Latest role of intervention combined with systemic therapy**
- The 2026 Pan-Asian ESMO guideline allows “TACE + immunotherapy + anti-angiogenic therapy” to be considered for some intermediate-stage HCC, but long-term benefit is not established and it is not a uniform standard for all intermediate-stage HCC. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13542233/?utm_source=openai))
- In the original phase III EMERALD-1 study, median progression-free survival with TACE plus durvalumab and bevacizumab was 15.0 months versus 8.2 months in the control arm, HR 0.77; **the PFS improvement in this report is not the same as a proven overall-survival benefit**. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12282661/?utm_source=openai))

### 4. Systemic therapy: the main path for advanced disease and when intervention is unsuitable or has failed

**Main conditions**
- Macrovascular invasion or extrahepatic metastasis;
- or disease confined to the liver that cannot be cured, is unsuitable for intervention, or has progressed after intervention.
- The strongest evidence comes from **Child–Pugh A, ECOG 0–1** populations; Child–Pugh B needs careful selection, and trial results cannot simply be applied to decompensated cirrhosis. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

**Regimen framework**
- Immunotherapy combinations include atezolizumab + bevacizumab and durvalumab + tremelimumab; the Pan-Asian guideline also includes options such as nivolumab + ipilimumab.
- When an immunotherapy combination is unsuitable, targeted drugs such as lenvatinib or sorafenib can be considered.
- Later lines depend on earlier exposure and tolerance; the best sequence after an immunotherapy combination is not settled. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13542233/?utm_source=openai))

**Checks needed before treatment**
- Bevacizumab-containing regimens: varices and recent bleeding, treating high-risk varices first if needed; also assess blood pressure, proteinuria and similar.
- Immunotherapy: autoimmune disease, organ-transplant history, immunosuppressive drugs and risk of immune-related toxicity.
- All regimens need blood count, liver and kidney function and viral hepatitis status. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

## 3. Response assessment and switching paths

- **Local treatment should not be judged on tumour diameter alone**: contrast CT/MRI should assess residual viable tissue, usually with mRECIST; the AFP trend only helps. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13542233/?utm_source=openai))
- **Systemic therapy**: imaging response, toxicity, liver function and ECOG together decide whether to continue, switch or stop; clinical trials mainly use RECIST 1.1. ([easlcampus.eu](https://easlcampus.eu/sites/default/files/2025-02/EASL_CPG_Management_HCC.pdf))
- **Reassess the chance of cure after downstaging**, but “shrinkage on imaging” does not automatically mean safe resection or transplant eligibility. ([easlcampus.eu](https://easlcampus.eu/sites/default/files/2025-02/EASL_CPG_Management_HCC.pdf))
- **Adjuvant systemic therapy should not be added by default after curative treatment**: neither EASL 2025 nor the 2026 Pan-Asian ESMO guideline recommends routine adjuvant systemic therapy after resection or ablation, so the related recommendation in the earlier AASLD 2023 version should not be applied directly. ([easlcampus.eu](https://easlcampus.eu/sites/default/files/2025-02/EASL_CPG_Management_HCC.pdf))

Another branch that must not be missed is **liver transplant**: early HCC with clinically significant portal hypertension or decompensation should be assessed for transplant rather than defaulting to TACE or systemic therapy; for patients who cannot have a transplant and have very poor liver function or performance status, supportive care and symptom control matter. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/10663390/?utm_source=openai))

2. **AASLD Practice Guidance on prevention, diagnosis, and treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma.** 2023. ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10663390/?utm_source=openai))

**Conclusion: Layer A leans to S4 (cannot judge).** Two TACE sessions are a trigger for reassessment, not evidence of treatment failure; the history of ascites means current liver reserve needs checking.

**Visible course:** E1 (day -107) TACE for hepatocellular carcinoma, with chronic hepatitis B and ascites recorded; E2 (day -59) repeat TACE, with cirrhosis recorded. **Layer B: when each applies — what to check**

| Action family | When it applies — what to check |
|---|---|
| Continue TACE | Prior benefit, a viable lesion still to embolize, and tolerated — imaging response, liver reserve |
| Adjust TACE | Residual disease with correctable under-embolization — feeding arteries, previous embolization extent |
| Systemic or combination therapy | Clear progression or unsuitable for further embolization — invasion, metastasis, liver function and performance status |
| HAIC or radiotherapy | Intrahepatic disease unsuitable for further embolization — blood supply, target and normal-liver reserve |
| Curative assessment | May meet criteria for resection, ablation or transplant — tumour number, size, location, liver reserve and transplant eligibility |
| Palliative support | Symptom burden or poor tolerance of anticancer treatment — current ascites, performance status and patient goals |
| Gather missing data first | Response or tolerance unclear (this node) — retrieve contrast imaging, intervention records and labs |
| Refer to MDT | Chance of cure or strategy switch disputed — collect staging and tolerance data |

**When to reassess:** before the treatment decision on Day 0, compare contrast imaging before and after the two TACE sessions, check current ascites control, bilirubin, albumin, coagulation and performance status, then judge Layer A again.
